depictions.what: more sodium drawn in the extracellular fluid than in the intracellular fluid
more potassium drawn in the intracellular fluid than in the extracellular fluid
the pump drawn in the cell membrane, moving ions across it
each ion carried from the side where it is at a lower concentration to the side where it is at a higher concentration: sodium outward, potassium inward
an energy symbol on the pump, because moving against a concentration gradient needs energy

sources.quote: An example of active transport is the sodium-potassium pump, which uses energy to maintain higher levels of sodium in the extracellular fluid and higher levels of potassium in the intracellular fluid.
sources.section: 15.2 Basic Fluid and Electrolyte Concepts, Solute Movement

sources.quote: Active transport, unlike diffusion, involves moving solutes and ions across a cell membrane from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration.
sources.section: 15.2 Basic Fluid and Electrolyte Concepts, Solute Movement

sources.quote: Because active transport moves solutes against a concentration gradient to prevent an overaccumulation of solutes in an area, energy is required for this process to take place.
sources.section: 15.2 Basic Fluid and Electrolyte Concepts, Solute Movement

sources.quote: Recall that sodium (Na+) is the primary electrolyte in the extracellular space and potassium (K+) is the primary electrolyte in the intracellular space.
sources.section: 15.2 Basic Fluid and Electrolyte Concepts, Solute Movement
